Pages 2–15 · Gram-Negative Architecture + Endotoxin

Three broad metabolic buckets

Enterobacteriaceae: facultative anaerobic glucose fermenters.

Non-fermenters: use aerobic respiration rather than fermenting glucose.

Anaerobic bacteria: ferment under oxygen-free conditions.

Envelope logic

Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane. The deck emphasizes LPS, porins, and the periplasmic space as major functional differences from Gram-positive bacteria.

Page 15. The faculty summary labels outer membrane, inner membrane, peptidoglycan, LPS, porin channels, periplasmic space, and lipid A in one diagram.
LPS = Lipid A + core polysaccharide + O-side chain.

Lipid A

Anchors LPS to the outer membrane and is the toxic portion associated with fever, WBC changes, shock, and DIC.

Core

Contains the conserved sugars KDO and heptoses. The deck calls KDO highly conserved among Gram-negative rods.

O-side chain

Repeating polysaccharide units that vary among organisms and contribute to adherence/colonization.

Page 6. Lipid A is shown as the membrane-anchoring LPS component associated with fever, leukocyte changes, shock, and DIC.
Exam anchor: Lipid A = toxic anchor. Core = KDO + heptoses. O-side chain = variable outer antigen.

Outer membrane, porins, and periplasm

The outer membrane is an asymmetric phospholipid/LPS bilayer and acts as a permeability barrier. Porins permit small hydrophilic solutes. The periplasm contains binding proteins plus detoxifying/hydrolytic enzymes such as β-lactamases.

Pages 16–22 · Enterobacteriaceae

Page 16. The defining cluster emphasized by Fisher: facultative anaerobes, all ferment glucose, all reduce nitrate to nitrite, and all are cytochrome-oxidase negative; lactose fermentation varies.
Enterobacteriaceae = glucose fermenter + nitrate reducer + oxidase negative. Lactose fermentation is the variable feature used later on MacConkey agar.

Cytochrome oxidase significance

Enterobacteriaceae lack cytochrome c oxidase and therefore test oxidase negative. The deck contrasts this directly with oxidase-positive Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Conjugation

The sex pilus can transfer plasmid DNA, and the lecture explicitly connects this with antibiotic resistance.

Fimbriae: attachment determines site

The deck links fimbrial attachment to GI mucosa (traveler’s diarrhea), uroepithelium (UTI), and the choroid plexus (neonatal meningitis).

ETEC toxins

Heat-labile toxin → ↑ cAMP → chloride secretion → sodium follows → osmotic diarrhea.

Heat-stable toxin → ↑ cGMP → the same net secretory-diarrhea logic.

Shiga toxin association

E. coli O157:H7 and Shigella dysenteriae are associated in the deck with bloody diarrhea and hemolytic-uremic syndrome / microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

Pages 23–27 · Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Page 23. The deck’s core laboratory profile: aerobic, oxidase positive, soil/water habitat, blue-green pyocyanin pigment, and grape-like odor.

Versus Enterobacteriaceae

P. aeruginosa is a non-fermenter and oxidase positive; Enterobacteriaceae ferment glucose and are oxidase negative.

Ecology

Fisher explicitly places P. aeruginosa in soil and water.

Page 25. Virulence is presented as a layered package: relatively impermeable outer membrane, fimbriae, endotoxin, cytotoxins/hemolysins, inactivating enzymes, efflux pumps, and biofilm.

Proteolytic enzymes

Elastase damages respiratory epithelium/collagen. Alkaline protease is shown blocking TNF-α and IFN-γ, lysing fibrin, and damaging cornea.

Exotoxin A + exoenzyme S

The lecture compares exotoxin A with diphtheria toxin and shows inhibition of elongation factor-2 / protein synthesis. Exoenzyme S is labeled as impairing phagocytosis.

Ozzy hiding spot: Lecture 4 puts him in the Pseudomonas section rather than the same fixed location used in earlier builds.

Pages 28–40 · Diagnostic Microbiology + Common Enterics

Culture → identification workflow shown in the deck

Fisher walks from streaking for isolation and blood/MacConkey agar through BacTAlert, BioFire multiplex PCR, MALDI-TOF MS, and susceptibility testing. The point is not one single technology; it is the sequence from detection → rapid organism identification → culture-based confirmation/susceptibility.

Page 30. MacConkey agar is both selective and differential: bile salts + crystal violet suppress Gram-positive growth, lactose is the sole carbohydrate, and neutral red reports acid production.
Lactose fermentation → acidic environment (pH < 6.8) → red/pink colony area. No lactose fermentation → no red color.
Page 37. The comparison slide emphasizes E. coli as motile and Klebsiella pneumoniae as non-motile with a thick capsule.

E. coli

Motile; lactose-positive on MacConkey in the examples; clinically tied earlier to GI disease, UTI, and neonatal meningitis.

Klebsiella pneumoniae

Non-motile, lactose fermenting, and notable for a thick capsule.

Shigella vs Salmonella typhi

Shigella: non-motile; dysentery. S. typhi: motile; typhoid fever.

Serratia marcescens

Shown as an oxidase-negative enteric organism with characteristic red pigment in some strains.

Page 39. Proteus mirabilis: swarming motility and urease positivity; urea splitting raises urine pH and is linked to kidney stones.

Pages 41–47 · Gram-Negative Anaerobes

Microbiome crossover. The deck briefly calls the microbiome the “forgotten organ” and identifies Bacteroidetes as dominant Gram-negative anaerobes. This lecture-specific mention does not replace the separate Week 9 self-paced microbiome session.
Page 42. Bacteroides/Gram-negative anaerobes are shown using an anaerobic electron-transport chain with nitrate rather than oxygen as the final electron acceptor; many make β-lactamase and contain endotoxin.

Where they live

The lecture emphasizes mucosal sites, especially mouth and colon, where anaerobes can greatly outnumber aerobes.

Named groups

Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Prevotella, and Veillonella.

Virulence package

Resistance to oxygen toxicity (catalase / superoxide dismutase), collagenases, capsule, fimbriae, endotoxin, and immunoglobulin proteases.

Page 46. Faculty clinical clues for anaerobic infection: infection near a mucosal surface, mixed flora on Gram stain, malodor, and tissue gas.

Anaerobic culture methods

The deck shows thioglycolate broth, an anaerobic jar with blood agar plates, and cooked chopped-meat broth.

LO Review · What You Should Be Able to Do

Identify the wall

Recognize the Gram-negative outer membrane, LPS, porins, thin peptidoglycan, periplasm, and inner membrane.

Decode endotoxin

Lipid A = toxic anchor; core = KDO/heptoses; O-side chain = variable outer antigen.

Recognize Enterobacteriaceae

Facultative anaerobes, glucose fermentation, nitrate reduction, oxidase negative; lactose fermentation varies.

Use MacConkey correctly

Selective against Gram-positive organisms and differential for lactose fermentation.

Separate E. coli from Pseudomonas

E. coli fits the enteric fermenter/oxidase-negative framework; Pseudomonas is a non-fermenter, oxidase positive, soil/water organism with pyocyanin and grape-like odor.

Know the ecology actually taught

Enterics are GI-associated; Pseudomonas is soil/water; anaerobic GNR are emphasized at mucosal sites. Use ScholarRx for the additional LO-listed groups not fully developed in this deck.

Last 60 seconds: Gram− = outer membrane + LPS + porin + periplasm · Lipid A = toxic anchor · Enterobacteriaceae = ferment glucose / nitrate+ / oxidase− · MacConkey = bile + crystal violet, lactose + neutral red · Pseudomonas = non-fermenter / oxidase+ / blue-green / grape odor / soil-water · Proteus = swarming + urease · anaerobic infection = mucosa + mixed flora + malodor + gas.
